title: How do you make a good game with the help of ai and not be seen as a slop gamedev?
author: Any-Landscape434
selftext:
Just wondering what ways ai should be used and when it shouldn't? how do you make a game using ai without it being bad or being seen as negative?

Also where do you all post your projects at for feedback and such? i want to make a game but i have no clue how to code, should i use ai?

comments.author: fellingzonders
comments.body: Ask your ai

comments.author: Blake9712
comments.body: You can disclose that ai helped or did all the programming but if you can either hand make or source the artwork without ai and wait it out a bit you should be fine. Just about everything is programmed with ai tho. I’d say the only way to avoid backlash is to avoid ai art and have a unique idea

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: Good game design

comments.author: LoCal_GwJ
comments.body: learn how to be an actual game developer so that you know what to do and aren't relying on an LLM to do everything for you

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
I don't want to sound like an ass, but if you have to ask.. you don't know what you're doing. Have fun with it, by all means practice, but if you don't know what makes a game good, how are you going to make a good game?

Again, not gatekeeping here. But you're trying to be a great songwriter by asking "how do I be a great songwriter?" while using a machine that generates songs. You're kind of missing the point.

replies.author: Whoa1Whoa1
replies.body: This. And for OP, stop thinking of a game as either made by AI or not made by AI. AI can help you make art or models or textures or music or code or even help you brainstorm ideas. It's very formulaic and unoriginal. A game with great visuals is not necessarily a good game. You gotta have a great game loop that feels amazing to play. If it's a platformer, it better have amazing controls and movement that feels sick. If the movement sucks or the animation of the character feels off, you need to keep working on that until it's perfect. And then you can implement your actual twist on a platformer game. Mario has power ups and worlds and funny enemies. Donkey Kong is more serious and you die in two hits. Sonic is fast and has to choose between rolling or dashing or jumping. And so forth. What would your game add to the genre that doesn't exist so far? If you can't answer that, then there is no point in having AI generate anything.

replies.author: jaykal001
replies.body:
This is my take away as well.

The big negative is that somebody is trying to crank out a game, fully built with AI, that isn't fun, there's no hook, it's not bug free, it's not engaging, etc.  It's none of the things that people who enjoy games look for.  It's seen as a fast-track to try to publish something to make a buck.

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
ChatGPT, how do I make a viral youtube video?

In all seriousness, this is the answer.  Game *design* is paramount.  No tools make up for a bad design.  You can hire all the developers and artists and musicians you want and still pump out a shit game if the design isn't there, or you can make a fantastic game with stick figures and greyboxes if the design rocks.  People here tend to get way too hung up on the media assets when the design is like 90% of the battle.

comments.author: Obvious_Catch_3034
comments.body:
There is no "AI make me a full polished game". You'll still need to do work and have a good design, idea, mechanics, etc.  
  
Look at your game > Does a part of it look like AI slop / AI generated? > If so iterate on and improve that part. 

Also if you don't know how to code but can make art you have the advantage. Most people only care about what they see and hear when it comes to AI in games. The majority of players couldn't care less about the code. You'll see some coders (like me) cope about the flaws with AI code but it doesn't matter in most games. Players didn't care when indie games were held together by a page of 1000 if statements.

replies.author: DudeWithASweater
replies.body: Yep, even with AI doing all the heavy lifting you still have to actually have an eye for game design and you absolutely need to iterate constantly.

replies.author: R3DB71ND
replies.body: And sound design. I’m quickly finding out that SFX are hard AF to do right without your game sounding like a high school project.

comments.author: dilberry
comments.body:
I notice that character animation / movement is the first slop attack target - right away you can tell if the main character(s) are rigid upright poorly rigged 3d models made by AI, with odd movements/weird swing animations, weird arm movements, etc. 

Claude and GPT are honestly total garbage at rigging these things without very specific instruction and iteration

comments.author: SaltyVon
comments.body: You don't. People who don't like AI to the point of calling even a whiff of it slop already won't have their mind changed even if you made something revolutionary. You're five years too early to be talking about AI being in your game as an indie. Hopefully by then it'll be more accepted. Until then, there's no bad way to use AI so long as you aren't ripping or stealing from other people's creations. Use it to your heart's content.

comments.author: siberianmi
comments.body:
AI has no taste for gameplay and will simply deliver something that mechanically generally works.

You have to make it fun.  That’s it.  That’s all.

Assets don’t matter.  
How much AI coded don’t matter.

Is the game loop good.  The end.

comments.author: zayelion
comments.body:
I was just about to answer this with a different post. Its doing the process with 2 humans. One running the AI the other reviewing everything. Standard Dev-QA team work. When I say everything I mean everything. Often both of us. I review initially then they do.

A QA isnt a normal human you pull of the street. They are a very special person that understands enough technicals to express what is wrong and suggest a fix. Often within a few edits of what could be considered a prompt to a higher level AI. 

The idea of a "normal" person looking at a game is actually horrifying and I have deep trauma from it because a "normal" person would not tell you much. Imagine you build a rollercoaster out of wood and you need to have it safety inspected. The inspector shows up, hits their foot on the curb because they are drunk in flipflops outside and then spends the next how ever long the session is belittling you about that they hit their foot outside the theme park and that its not safe. No review of mechanics. Actual safety. No appreciation at all. 

QA test just the thing, make sure just the thing works as intented, then gives a seperate queue for "precieved annoyance" they know its precieved, and dont belittle you to change the game into exactly the way they said. They give you space to think or not address it until other things are solid. They gently remind you. They do everything gently.

But they are the ones that find and point out the things that make something "feel sloppy" be it AI or human slop.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: practice and standards, look at the game outside of your self, have others no working with ai who you trust,. the biggest issue I see with people here they are amazed at what they are able to do, but the quality is no where near what most people would find enjoyable. ai is a tool, if you just go " make me game, make me money, don't bother me" your game will be bad.

comments.author: GoGs0l0dev
comments.body:
You could spend months iterating, playtesting, carefully curating each UI, game system, system inter connectivity, balancing the game loop, and improving the art design…

And some dude is still going to say it’s AI slop and not art for their 300 upvotes in a sub, no different than the one shot Frogger clone where frogger and all the other objects are just circles…

90% of gamers don’t give a fuck and just want to find games they want to play at reasonable prices.

If you are worried about public perception, your focus on making your game quality and not “slop” which to me just reads as something where no love, attention/care, QA/QC, or real effort was put in.

comments.author: phiiiiiiii
comments.body: Human intent, attention to details, sound architecture.

comments.author: FactorWonderful5085
comments.body:
Honestly the line between "using AI well" and slop comes down to one thing: whether you still apply taste and actually iterate, or just ship whatever it spits out on the first try.

I just finished a browser extraction shooter made almost entirely with AI, so from experience:

Where AI is genuinely great: systems and plumbing. The economy, the inventory grid, the save system, a server-authoritative anti-cheat, even the whole deploy (it runs free on an Oracle free VM behind Caddy with auto HTTPS). Tedious stuff that AI nails.

Where you earn your keep - and where slop shows: anything with feel. First-person hand poses were a multi-session nightmare: posing in Blender is easy, getting it into the engine without a deformed mess is not. Enemy AI too - a state machine is easy, making it actually feel smart (react to being shot, take cover, not freeze in the open) took endless iteration and it's still rough. Skip that iteration and that's the slop people smell.

So: treat AI as a fast junior dev and yourself as the director who says "no, that's wrong, do it again." The caring is the part that isn't automatable.

On "I can't code": yes, start with AI, but read what it writes and fix its mistakes yourself - that's how you actually learn instead of being stuck the moment it breaks.

Put mine online free if you want a rough-but-real example - you just pick any username + password to log in (no email; it only saves your progress on the server, which I did on purpose to avoid any privacy/legal headaches): [https://extraction.worldai.it/](https://extraction.worldai.it/)

comments.author: BSwayzeYo
comments.body: Just make a good game that you’re proud of, and don’t rush to market. The AI haters are fading into history. Give it some more time.

comments.author: Klutzy-Wall-3560
comments.body:
The hard part of game design was never writing code. The hard part was always having good ideas. So the solution is to have original ideas which have value. That value is proved by what you make. 

If you are worried that somebody else could come along and build your game based off of a tagline or just “the idea“ leaking then you are probably lacking steps 2-1,000,000 in the creative process, which happen step by step as you make the game.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
You have to have a lot of related skills, like art and game design and programming, or you have to work with people that have those skills. 

AI doesn’t make art skills obsolete. Same with programming.

comments.author: XalAtoh
comments.body:
After checking your profile... I give you a genuine advice... don't bother making a game *for other people*.

Sure, pay an AI subscription and built games for YOURSELF and people around you. But with your boring personality, lack of creative mind, lack thinking skills and your lack of general game-dev related talents... just don't.

But it seems you are just bored and want to do something, in that case, sure, take an AI subscription, just don't expect anyone to like your game... not gonna happen.

replies.author: aigamedev-ModTeam
replies.body: Be respectul to others and follow reddits guidelines and policies.

comments.author: ChaosMilkTea
comments.body:
Think of it like this: "If I had a team of people making the game for me, how would I make sure the game was good?"

A good idea you polish and refine through testing and effort.

comments.author: TechgeekOne
comments.body:
Same way we did it before AI. AI is a force multiplier, it's not a magic "make it good" tool. You still need to handle the vision, direction, polish, and design aspects to ensure the end result looks good, plays well, and is fun. AI can definitely help fill gaps or get you to a result faster but it's not capable of replacing the higher level aspects of game creation just yet.

Keep in mind someone is still probably going to be pissed you used AI at this point because it's a hot topic. Unless they have real constructive criticism that isn't just "learn to do it yourself n00b" I'd just ignore them.

comments.author: MattMaxBuilds
comments.body: Playtest early and often. If you don't have fun or want to play your own game, it's likely others won't either.

comments.author: SolrayCultist
comments.body: I'm going to try to stick with my crap pixel art skills, so I'll have some human slop there too. Lol.

comments.author: GrimMilkMan
comments.body: I think we're at a point that if you develop fully with AI you have to put a product out that above and beyond the average of other games

comments.author: fhtiek
comments.body:
This is kind of a silly question. If you put the same effort, taste, playtesting and consistent artistic vision into an AI game as you would a handmade one then you are good.

Theres this massive focus in this and most other AI/vibecoding communities where everyone is trying to go as hands-off, one-shot, done in a weekend as possible, and thats the exact reason thise projects are slop. 

The difference with AI is you can act as a creative director rather than wearing every hat yourself. Creative director is a demanding job and if they dont do it well the game comes out slop, regardless of methodology.

If you shortcut, everybody knows. Its written all over the project

replies.author: Vindelator
replies.body: Yeah, if people replaced the expectation that a good game only takes a day to make and started measuring the time in years, you'd clear the slop problem up pretty fast.

replies.author: backagainlikeabadpen
replies.body: Yes same with AI-gen films and tv. Obviously it's great that we on are on the cusp of people being able to produce feature length films for just a month's salary (or even less!), at the same though people will need to spend the same amount of time doing research, writing, rewriting, editing, finessing, polishing etc.

replies.author: soulglider26
replies.body:
Unfortunately I don't think this is true. It's been tested in many places. 

Post something not made with AI that would be considered good otherwise. Tell people it's AI. They shit all over it.

Many people are anti AI no matter the outcome, especially on reddit. Not sure anywhere else outside of reddit though.

comments.author: pizzae
comments.body: What do you think: a “make no mistakes” prompt or 2000 hours of grinding? Which will make a better game beyond a one shot?

comments.author: Livid_Shallot5701
comments.body:
make it look stunning  and COHERENT, 

and make it be polished and optimized to INDUSTRY STANDARD

comments.author: primaldeed
comments.body: Python

comments.author: HaphazardlyOrganized
comments.body: I think that's what a lot of us are stuggling with in this new paradigm. I think part of it comes down to playing it a lot and trusting yourself to know if its fun or not.

comments.author: Total_Engineering_51
comments.body: Look up GMTK on YouTube and watch through his catalog. That gives you a decent start on thinking about how games are designed and what you can start directing agent sessions to do. Have the agents implement against known design patterns as you work through each problem space to help fight the tendency of AI to implement overly literally and create piles of spaghetti code in short order. That also means using an engine to help fence the agents in, Unity or Godot are probably the best bet here. I’d stay away from three.js except for fast prototypes and even then you’ll need to be careful in how you have the agents port into your final dev environment. Have a plan for graphics, sound and graphical elements/assets… the biggest blow back is here and this is your first impression… to paraphrase the culinary idiom, you play with your eyes first… if what they see looks like AI, all the biases kick in, even the more latent ones people will have. I feel like the most successful games that use AI will have different answers on this front and there won’t be a single, one sized fit for everyone.

comments.author: orbital_trace
comments.body: Make a fun game, don't tell people you used ai

comments.author: Dankenweenie
comments.body:
AI will always be seen as negative by luddites and thats just a reality we have to deal with until it becomes mainstream. 

To avoid being "slop" however then the simple measure is effort. Slop to me is clearly low effort where someone literally asked AI to "make x game" then pushed the entire game as is and their next question was "how to upload to Steam".

Put effort, care and time into your game and nobody should even be able to realise it was made with AI without you telling them.

comments.author: Strong_Ad6826
comments.body: Use Ai to collect your notes and help you make a GDD, then make a goddamn video game the way your target audience demands

comments.author: fluxtah
comments.body: Don't one shot, iterate, play test, if the idea is good it will grow to something undeniably great

comments.author: One_Salty_Pigeon
comments.body:
I mean if you use AI in a visible way the Anti AI crowd will always call it ai slop there's really no way around it. Like some have said if you do the art you'll be better off (tbh even some of the art is getting harder to spot if you do it right). But going into this I expect and fully anticipate getting plenty of 'AI Slop' comments when marketing my game and plan to ignore every last one. 

For the vast majority of people they don't really care about what you used or how you used it they just want to play a fun game with out to many bugs. If you can manage that then you're good.

If you 'one shot it' which I didn't even know was thing and create a crappy game than they won't call it slop they'll just call it crap.

Outside of that the flow is simple code, test, code, test, code, test code, test. Think how can I break this, how will other people break this, is this fun or just tedious, 

Good example I'm making a shop sim right now and I wanted to add having to get change for your cashiers... so far from testing I removed it because I haven't really found it to be a fun mechanic to deal with while playing. I've easily play tested my game in the last 2 weeks 20+ hours including 11 of just playing like a normal player to understand the progression of the game and how it feels. That is the reality of game dev AI or no AI it's testing and playing and tweaking it until the game feels good in every aspect.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body: I have reviewed 20 games so far and you can check out my videos if you want to see how other AI games are doing. dm me or check my post history for a link

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
The machine is just a tool (and maybe, increasingly, a sometimes-but-not-always helpful collaborator). The fundamentals of the process for making a good game have no changed just because there is a new tool. 

You need to prototype, you need to iterate, you need to build with intention and design with intention.

To me, the 'slop' I see is a consequence of someone just not understanding that fixating on something like smooth animations will not lead to a good game. You need the concept first, the actual core experience, and THEN you need things like a means of create smooth animations and gorgeous visuals and etc etc. You do need an art direction early, of course, and especially now you can make the game beautiful as you build it - but don't chase the content at the expense of the game. The game is the experience, the content is what elevates it.

Also, IMHO, if you approach any art with just, 'I want to make an art', I think you will probably fail. Art is much more a verb than a noun; a response to a deeper desire to create a thing in your head. If you don't have that and just want to make an art because, hey, that's a trend right now... I can't see how that could ever produce something worth existing (slop, in other words).

comments.author: JorgitoEstrella
comments.body:
Don't use generic ai art they have the same "ai style", use different loras or just create many enough and pick the most original.

Also AI voices are still way behind than humans in emotions.

comments.author: craigitsfriday
comments.body:
A lot of other people have made some really good points regarding OPs question on how to use AI. Though, not much traction on the second part of the question beyond "who cares" or "expect negativity". In an effort to frame it around potential profitability, OP can look at a few recent studies on public perception around AI use on Steam. I'm limiting this to Steam because mobile has its own set of problems for indies beyond AI use.

In general, 69% of players say they welcome disclosure of AI use in games, while 31% view disclosure negatively. [https://daily.dev/posts/dislike-ai-content-in-your-games-68-6-of-steam-users-disagree-with-you-says-survey-m3qfblarb](https://daily.dev/posts/dislike-ai-content-in-your-games-68-6-of-steam-users-disagree-with-you-says-survey-m3qfblarb) 

Since Valve now requires you to disclose your AI use both during dev or during runtime, the advice to not tell anyone is not really a viable option for those looking to keep a business running (I imagine if you are audited and found out, a ban from Steam is not good for business). Regarding public sentiment, players have shown more support for AI use in code generation than for creative efforts like genAI for art, music, voice acting or writing. [https://www.g2a.com/news/features/gaming-entries/what-players-think-about-ai-in-games/](https://www.g2a.com/news/features/gaming-entries/what-players-think-about-ai-in-games/)

So now for the not so great part. Ross Burton, a market analyst for Game Oracle recently shared that developers who disclose AI usage see roughly 50-53% lower engagement (reviews, sales, etc) than non-AI indie titles, regarding the AI mark as a scarlet letter.

So my question to devs who've shipped AI games, similar to OPs second question, is what's your process for marketing your games? Steam disclosure is one thing, but in your trailers, promo clips on social media, landing page are you disclosing that you are making an AI-assisted game or is it more of an answered if asked situation? I'm about a month into my current indie project (with 16 years making games professionally) and I'm wondering if the tried and true methods of marketing as an indie are still true in 2026 with aigamedev?

comments.author: Equivalent_Bird
comments.body: How to write a good book with the help of printer, and not be seen as a slop writer?

comments.author: drallcom3
comments.body:
> How do you make a good game with the help of ai and not be seen as a slop gamedev?

Make and finish a game. Learn from the feedback. Make another game.

comments.author: faxt-orial
comments.body: First of all kudos for trying. As long as you know what you want to build you can use AI to build it, but.. in the process you should make full use of AI to also learn how to code, that would help a lot further on. It just gets easier. I'd say you can use AI all over the place as long as you learn something new from it each time

comments.author: kadiotelki
comments.body: You would still need to put in work and be creative at least to get out the most of ai, otherwise it will look like slop

comments.author: Pale-Pangolin-9004
comments.body:
I think using AI for anything code-related is okay as it doesn't really make a difference so long as you understand the systems you're building. 

Anything with AI art seems to be the ones that get scrutinised the most as it sort of takes the heart and soul out of the project. 

But I think the best way to avoid being put in that category is to intentionally make a bad game. A game that's stupid, daft, makes no sense, but is still fun. 

Stuff like rock simulator, tree simulator, women simulator, games that are just stupid and were never intended to be taken seriously.

comments.author: UnironicallyDel
comments.body: You can definitely have ai \*help\* make a game. But mosst people do not do that. Letting ai make the whole game of even half of the game, is slop.

comments.author: Smart_Fix1947
comments.body:
There's no set-in-stone criteria, and the tech as well as surrounding culture/society is changing. My 2c: 

You have to be the final gate. A real, human gate on everything. Kind of like how AP News uses AI for their articles now but insists that a human reader must (in theory) look at everything so that it checks out. Slop is something that has not had this done---therefore users can expect to find obvious problems that a human being would have spotted (both errors/bugs and uncreative design choices, etc.).

comments.author: BlahajWithBenefits
comments.body:
If the game is good the game is good. 

If you made a fun game with a 5 word prompt and literally no other human input, they should be asking why they can’t make something better.
